title: Teach Programming in the IDE: Create Courses with the JetBrains Academy Plugin
subtitle: Build interactive programming courses that learners take inside PyCharm or IntelliJ IDEA, with tasks checked by tests and feedback that helps them learn.
outcomes: Explain why practising in a real IDE helps people learn to program
Install the JetBrains Academy plugin and take a course as a learner
Organise a course into lessons of theory tasks, programming tasks checked by tests, and quizzes
Write task descriptions, starter code and tests whose messages help learners fix their mistakes
Try a course as a learner, pilot it, improve it and share it
Design exercises that build skills step by step, with feedback that teaches
prerequisites: Comfort writing small Python programs and functions: the course's examples are in Python, and the same ideas work for Java and Kotlin in IntelliJ IDEA. You need PyCharm or IntelliJ IDEA (a free version is enough) with Python 3, and the free JetBrains Academy plugin, which the course shows you how to install.
description: Build programming courses that learners take inside a professional IDE. With the free JetBrains Academy plugin for PyCharm, IntelliJ IDEA and other JetBrains IDEs, every task in a course has a description, starter code and a Check button that runs your tests on the learner's code, so learners practise with real tools and get feedback straight away. You'll start by taking a course as a learner, then build your own: organising lessons and tasks, writing theory tasks and quizzes, and creating programming tasks with answer placeholders and tests whose messages tell learners exactly what to fix. You'll check your tests against the mistakes learners really make, try your course in a preview, pilot it with a real learner, and share it as an archive or on JetBrains Marketplace, learning along the way what makes exercises and feedback teach. The plugin's menus change between versions, so the course shows where things usually are and how to find any action by name. It ends with a mini-course of your own, built, tested and piloted.

modules.title: Why teach programming in the IDE
modules.summary: See why practising in a professional IDE helps people learn to program, install the JetBrains Academy plugin, and take a course the way your learners will.

lessons.title: Learning to program in a real IDE
objectives: Explain what learners gain by practising in a professional IDE
Describe what the JetBrains Academy plugin adds to an IDE
Install the plugin
key_points: Practising in a professional IDE means learners write, run and debug code with the tools they'll use at work, so nothing has to be relearnt when they move on from the course.
An IDE gives feedback while learners type: errors are underlined, names are completed and quick-fixes are offered, so learners can correct many small mistakes on their own.
The JetBrains Academy plugin, formerly called EduTools, turns an IDE project into an interactive course: each task has a description, starter code and a Check button.
Checking a programming task runs the author's tests on the learner's own computer and shows the result in the IDE, so learners can try again as often as they need.
Courses made with the plugin can be taken in IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm and other JetBrains IDEs, in languages such as Python, Java and Kotlin.

steps.do: Open Settings and go to Plugins.
On the Marketplace tab, search for JetBrains Academy and click Install. If it's already on the Installed tab, make sure it's enabled.
Restart the IDE if it asks you to.
Open Find Action and type course to see the plugin's actions. Their names and places in the menus vary between versions, but Find Action always finds them.
steps.see: Actions such as Browse Courses and Create New Course.

steps.do: Open the course catalogue: from the Welcome screen it's on the Learn tab, and with a project open it's usually File | Learn and Teach | Browse Courses.

lessons.title: Taking a course as a learner
objectives: Work through a task the way a learner does
Read the feedback a failed check gives
Identify the parts of a task that its author writes
key_points: A course opens as an IDE project: the Project tool window lists its lessons and tasks, and the current task's description is shown in a panel beside the editor.
In a programming task, learners write code where the author left answer placeholders, the highlighted gaps in the starter code, and then click Check.
Check runs the author's tests against the learner's code and shows either that the task is solved or a message from a test that failed.
Hints in a description stay folded until a learner opens one, so learners can take help a step at a time.

Everything learners see, from the description and starter code to the hints and the messages from failed tests, was written by the course's author: the quality of the feedback is in the author's hands.

walkthrough.title: Solve a task and read its feedback

steps.do: Open the course catalogue and start a free Python course for beginners. The IDE creates a project for it.
Open the Project tool window to see the course's lessons and tasks.
Open the first programming task. Read its description in the task panel, and find the answer placeholders in the editor.
Type a wrong answer on purpose and click Check in the task panel.
steps.see: The task isn't solved, and a message from the course's tests says why.

steps.do: Open a hint if the task has one, put your answer right and click Check again.
steps.see: The task is marked as solved.

steps.do: Go on to the next task with the button at the bottom of the task panel.

lab.title: Take a course as a learner, then plan yours
lab.goal: Install the JetBrains Academy plugin, solve three tasks of a course as a learner, note what helped and what got in the way, and plan the short Python course you'll build in this course's labs.
setup: PyCharm or IntelliJ IDEA (a free version is enough) with Python 3

steps.do: Install the JetBrains Academy plugin from Settings | Plugins, if it isn't installed already.
Open the course catalogue and start a free Python course.
Solve three tasks, at least one of them a programming task. Click Check at least once with a wrong answer, and open a hint if there is one.
Fill in learner_notes.md: the course and tasks, the message a failed check gave you, and what helped or got in the way, including IDE features such as completion or quick-fixes.

Plan your own course in course_plan.md: a short Python course for beginners, with its audience, three outcomes, and six tasks in order. Include at least one theory task, programming tasks and a quiz; the leap-years task you'll build in module 3 can be one of them.

checks.text: Three tasks of a course were taken, and the course is named.
The message from a failed check is quoted, with a judgement of whether it helped.
The plan names an audience and three outcomes that start with verbs.
The plan has six tasks in order, including theory, programming and quiz tasks, each with the idea it practises.

modules.title: Build a course: lessons, tasks and quizzes
modules.summary: Learn how a course is organised, create one in the IDE with lessons and tasks of each kind, and write theory tasks and quiz questions that teach.

lessons.title: How a course is organised
objectives: Describe how courses, lessons and tasks fit together
Choose the right kind of task for what learners should do
Explain what a task's folder holds
key_points: A course is made of lessons, which can be grouped into sections, and each lesson is a series of tasks that learners take in order.
A theory task explains an idea, often with code learners can run, and isn't checked; a programming task is checked by tests the author writes; a quiz asks a multiple-choice question.
The plugin has other kinds of task too, such as one checked by comparing a program's output with the output expected, and the names of task types differ between versions.
In a framework lesson, learners build one project across the lesson's tasks and their code carries on from task to task, which suits a guided project.
Each task is a folder holding its description (task.md in recent versions), the files learners work on, its tests, and a task-info.yaml file where the plugin keeps the task's settings.

steps.do: In the course you took in module 1, open the Project tool window.
steps.see: Lessons, and the tasks inside them, marked as solved or not.

steps.do: Expand a lesson and open a theory task, then a programming task, and compare their task panels.
steps.see: The theory task has no Check button to pass; the programming task does.

steps.do: Find a quiz task, if the course has one, and answer it.
steps.see: Options to choose from, and a check of your choice.

steps.do: Use Search Everywhere to jump to a task's file by name, such as task.py.

lessons.title: Create a course in the IDE
objectives: Create a new course project with the plugin
Add lessons and tasks of different kinds
Find the plugin's actions when its menus differ
key_points: Creating a course makes a project in course creator mode, where you add, rename and reorder lessons and tasks and edit everything learners will see.

You choose a course's language when you create it, and it decides the files and tests new tasks get: in recent versions, Python tasks get unittest tests, and Java and Kotlin courses use Gradle and JUnit.
New lessons and tasks are added from the right-click menu in the Project tool window, and their order there is the order learners meet them in.

The plugin keeps the settings of the course, each lesson and each task in YAML files (course-info.yaml, lesson-info.yaml and task-info.yaml) beside the content, so a course can live in Git like any project.
The plugin's menus have changed between versions: if an item isn't where you expect it, Find Action finds it by name, such as Create New Course.

walkthrough.title: Create a course with a lesson and three tasks

steps.do: Start a new course: File | Learn and Teach | Create New Course, or open Find Action and type Create New Course.
Give the course a title, Python Warm-ups, a short description and the language Python, then create it.
steps.see: A project in course creator mode, usually with a first lesson and task already in place.

steps.do: In the Project tool window, rename the first lesson to warm_ups.
Right-click the lesson and choose New | Task. Name it welcome and choose the theory type.
Add two more tasks the same way: even_or_odd, a programming task (called an Edu task in some versions), and which_type, a quiz (a multiple-choice or choice task in some versions).
Open even_or_odd's files.
steps.see: task.md for the description, task.py for the code, and tests/test_task.py for the tests.

lessons.title: Theory tasks and quizzes
objectives: Write a theory task around an example learners can run
Write a multiple-choice question whose wrong options teach
Explain wrong answers in feedback
key_points: A theory task introduces one idea with a short explanation and an example learners can run and change; it isn't checked, so keep it short and lead straight into practice.
A good quiz question tests one idea and can't be answered by spotting a pattern in its wording.
Wrong options, called distractors, work best when each is a mistake learners really make, such as thinking that "7" + "3" gives 10 rather than "73".
A quiz can have one correct option or several; say in the question how many to choose.
Feedback on a wrong answer should explain the misunderstanding behind it, not only that it was wrong.

walkthrough.title: Write a theory task and a quiz

steps.do: Open the welcome task's task.md and write a short explanation in Markdown.
steps.code:
# Numbers and text

Python treats `7` and `"7"` differently: the first is a number and the second is text, called a string.
`+` adds numbers but joins strings. Run `task.py` to see both.

steps.do: Put the example in the task's code file, so learners can run it.
Run the file to check the example.
steps.see: 10, then 73.

steps.do: Open which_type and write its question: What does print("7" + "3") show? Give four options, 10, 73, 7 + 3 and an error, with 73 as the only correct one. Depending on the version, you set the options in a form or in the task's task-info.yaml.
Read the task panel to see the question as learners will.

lab.title: Build the skeleton of your course
lab.goal: Create a Python course with one lesson of three tasks, a theory task, a programming task checked by tests and a quiz, and print its structure.
setup: PyCharm or IntelliJ IDEA with the JetBrains Academy plugin and Python 3
Download show_course.py, and keep it outside the course's folder

steps.do: Create a new Python course called Python Warm-ups. If the menu item isn't where the lesson showed, use Find Action and type Create New Course.
Rename the first lesson to warm_ups, and give it three tasks in this order: welcome (theory), even_or_odd (programming) and which_type (quiz).
In welcome, write a short description of numbers and strings, and put the example in its code file.
In even_or_odd, describe the task in task.md (write is_even(n), which returns True for an even number and False for an odd one), and put this solution in task.py.
Replace the example test in tests/test_task.py with these two tests.
Select return n % 2 == 0, right-click and choose Add Answer Placeholder (it may be in a submenu named after the plugin or Course Creator). Use pass as the placeholder text.
Run the tests from the Terminal in the task's folder.
steps.code:
cd warm_ups/even_or_odd
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
steps.see: Ran 2 tests, then OK.

steps.do: Write the quiz in which_type: what print("7" + "3") shows, with 73 as the one correct option and three distractors based on real mistakes.
From the course's top folder, print the course's structure.
steps.see: warm_ups with its three task folders, and even_or_odd holding task.md, task.py and tests/test_task.py.

checks.text: The lesson holds the three tasks.
The programming task has tests, and they pass against the solution.
The tests check exact values and have messages for learners.
The quiz's question and options are given, with the correct one marked.

lab.submit: Paste the output of show_course.py, the output of the test run, your tests/test_task.py, and the quiz's question and options, marking the correct one with (correct).
hints: If a new task has different files from the ones described, such as no tests folder, check the course's language and the task's type: names and defaults differ between versions.
python -m unittest discover -s tests runs every test file in tests whose name starts with test.

modules.title: Programming tasks and the tests that check them
modules.summary: Write task descriptions learners can follow, starter code with answer placeholders, and tests that check the work and say what's wrong when it isn't right.

lessons.title: Task descriptions learners can follow
objectives: Structure a task description: goal, examples and edge cases
Add hints that help a step at a time
Write in plain, precise language
key_points: A task description says what to write in its first sentence, then gives the details: the function's name and parameters, what it returns, and examples of inputs with their expected results.
Examples, such as a table of years and whether each is a leap year, show exactly what's expected and answer many questions before learners have to ask them.
Say which cases matter, such as negative numbers or an empty list, so that learners aren't marked wrong for something the description never mentioned.

Descriptions are written in Markdown; in recent versions of the plugin, a hint is a block written as
...
, which stays folded until a learner opens it.
Order hints from a gentle nudge to a near-solution, so learners take only as much help as they need.

walkthrough.title: Write a description with examples and hints

steps.do: Add a programming task named leap_years to the warm_ups lesson: right-click the lesson and choose New | Task.
Open its task.md and write the description: what to write, the rules, a table of examples, and two hints.
steps.code:
# Leap years A leap year has 366 days instead of 365. Write the function `is_leap_year(year)`, which returns `True` if `year` is a leap year and `False` if it isn't. The calendar's rules: - a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, - except a year divisible by 100, which isn't, - except a year divisible by 400, which is. | Year | Leap year? | |------|------------| | 2024 | yes | | 2023 | no | | 1900 | no | | 2000 | yes |
The % operator gives the remainder of a division, so year % 4 == 0 is true when the year is divisible by 4.
Check the most specific rule first: is the year divisible by 400?

steps.do: Read the description in the task panel, as learners will see it.
steps.see: The table, and the two hints folded until they're opened.

steps.do: Reformat the Markdown file if its table has gone ragged.

lessons.title: Starter code and answer placeholders
objectives: Write starter code that runs before learners change it
Mark what learners write with answer placeholders
Decide how big each gap should be
key_points: In course creator mode, a task's files hold your solution; an answer placeholder hides part of it and shows learners the placeholder's text instead.
Learners see the placeholder text, such as pass or a comment saying what to write, in place of your code; the rest of the starter code can show good style.
Starter code that runs, even if it gives the wrong answer, lets learners click Check straight away and get feedback instead of a syntax error.
One placeholder per idea keeps a task focused: a gap of an expression or a few lines suits beginners, and bigger gaps suit later tasks.
Check a task as its author first: the tests should pass with your solution and fail with the placeholder text in its place.

steps.do: Write the reference solution in leap_years' task.py.
Select the function's body; Extend Selection grows the selection a step at a time.
Right-click the selection and choose Add Answer Placeholder (in some versions it's in a submenu named after the plugin or Course Creator). Enter pass as the placeholder text.
steps.see: The body is highlighted as a placeholder.

steps.do: Click Check in the task panel. In course creator mode, the tests run against your solution.
steps.see: The task passes.

lessons.title: Tests that check the work and teach
objectives: Write unittest tests that check what a description asks for
Write failure messages that help learners fix their code
Check that tests catch the mistakes learners really make
key_points: In recent versions, a Python task's tests are ordinary unittest tests in its tests folder; when one fails, its message is the feedback the learner sees.
Test what the description promises, including edge cases such as 1900 and 2000 for leap years, not how the code is written: a correct solution that differs from yours must pass.
A good failure message says what was tested, what was expected and why, such as: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it isn't a leap year.
assertTrue passes for any value that counts as true, even the string 'no'; assertIs(result, True) or assertEqual checks the exact value.
Predict the mistakes learners will make, such as printing a result instead of returning it, write each as a wrong answer, and make sure a test fails for it with a message that helps.
Keep tests fast and independent, so Check answers in moments and one failure doesn't hide another.

steps.do: Open tests/test_task.py in the leap_years task.
Add tests to the test class, each with a message written for learners.
steps.code:
def test_a_century_is_not_a_leap_year(self):
        self.assertIs(is_leap_year(1900), False,
                      msg="1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400, so it isn't a leap year. "
                          "Check the 100 rule after the 4 rule.")

    def test_the_answer_is_returned_not_printed(self):
        self.assertIsNotNone(is_leap_year(2024),
                             msg="is_leap_year returned None. Use return to give back True or False; "
                                 "print only shows a value.")

steps.do: Run the tests with the green arrow beside the class, or run the test at the caret.
steps.see: The tests pass against your solution.

steps.do: Break the solution on purpose: delete the 400 rule's two lines and run the tests again. Read the failure as a learner would.
steps.see: A failed test whose message explains the rule that was broken.

steps.do: Put the solution back with Edit | Undo, and run the tests once more.

lab.title: Write a checked task with feedback that helps

setup: Your Python Warm-ups course from module 2
Download the starter files: leap_years (the task's files) and checker (a script and three wrong answers). Keep checker outside the course's folder.

steps.do: Add a programming task named leap_years to the warm_ups lesson. Replace its task.md, task.py and tests/test_task.py with the starter files from leap_years.
Put an answer placeholder over the body of is_leap_year, with pass as its text.
In the Terminal, from the course's top folder, run the checker on your task. It runs your tests against the reference solution and then against each wrong answer.
steps.see: reference solution passes all 1 test, then 1 of 3 wrong answers caught: the one starter test only catches the answer that prints instead of returning.

steps.do: Write the tests the TODO comments describe: a year that isn't divisible by 4, 1900, 2000, and a test whose message helps a learner who printed the answer instead of returning it. Use assertIs, so that a value such as 'yes' can't pass as True.
Run the checker again, and improve your messages until each wrong answer's messages would tell a learner what to fix.

checks.text: The tests pass the reference solution.
All three typical wrong answers are caught.
The tests check exact values with assertIs and cover the century rules.
Each test has a message that explains the rule, not just that the answer was wrong.
A message helps a learner who printed the answer instead of returning it.

lab.submit: Paste your tests/test_task.py and the checker's full output from its last run.

files.content:
# Leap years A leap year has 366 days instead of 365. Write the function `is_leap_year(year)`, which returns `True` if `year` is a leap year and `False` if it isn't. The calendar's rules: - a year divisible by 4 is a leap year, - except a year divisible by 100, which isn't, - except a year divisible by 400, which is. | Year | Leap year? | |------|------------| | 2024 | yes | | 2023 | no | | 1900 | no | | 2000 | yes |
The % operator gives the remainder of a division, so year % 4 == 0 is true when the year is divisible by 4.
Check the most specific rule first: is the year divisible by 400?

import unittest

from task import is_leap_year


class TestLeapYear(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_a_year_divisible_by_4_is_a_leap_year(self):
        self.assertIs(is_leap_year(2024), True,
                      msg="2024 is divisible by 4, so is_leap_year(2024) should return True.")

    # TODO: a year that isn't divisible by 4, such as 2023
    # TODO: a year divisible by 100 but not by 400, such as 1900, with a message that explains the rule
    # TODO: a year divisible by 400, such as 2000
    # TODO: a test whose message helps a learner who printed the answer instead of returning it

"""Run a task's tests against its reference solution and against typical wrong answers.

Good tests pass the reference solution and fail every wrong answer, with a message that helps the learner fix it.

Usage:   python try_wrong_answers.py path/to/task_folder
The task folder holds task.py (the reference solution) and tests/test_task.py. The wrong answers are the .py files
in the wrong_answers folder next to this script.
"""

import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def run_tests(task_folder: Path, solution: Path) -> tuple[int, int, list[str]]:
    """Run the task's tests with `solution` as task.py. Returns (tests run, tests failed, failure messages)."""
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
        work = Path(tmp)
        shutil.copy(solution, work / "task.py")
        shutil.copytree(task_folder / "tests", work / "tests")
        result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests"],
                                cwd=work, capture_output=True, text=True)
    output = result.stderr
    ran = re.search(r"Ran (\d+) tests?", output)
    failed = re.search(r"FAILED \((?:failures=(\d+))?(?:, )?(?:errors=(\d+))?", output)
    total = int(ran.group(1)) if ran else 0
    bad = sum(int(n) for n in failed.groups() if n) if failed else 0
    messages = [line.strip() for line in output.splitlines() if re.match(r"\w*(Error|Exception):", line.strip())]
    return total, bad, messages


def tests(n: int) -> str:
    return f"{n} test" if n == 1 else f"{n} tests"


def main() -> None:
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    task_folder = Path(sys.argv[1])
    total, bad, messages = run_tests(task_folder, task_folder / "task.py")
    if total == 0:
        sys.exit("No tests ran: is tests/test_task.py in the task folder?")
    if bad:
        print(f"reference solution FAILS {bad} of {tests(total)}: fix the tests or the solution first")
        for m in messages:
            print("    " + m)
        sys.exit(1)
    print(f"reference solution passes all {tests(total)}")

    wrong = sorted((HERE / "wrong_answers").glob("*.py"))
    caught = 0
    for answer in wrong:
        total, bad, messages = run_tests(task_folder, answer)
        if bad:
            caught += 1
            print(f"{answer.name}: caught, {bad} of {tests(total)} failed")
            for m in messages:
                print("    " + m)
        else:
            print(f"{answer.name}: NOT caught, every test passed")
    print(f"{caught} of {len(wrong)} wrong answers caught")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

def is_leap_year(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0

hints: If the reference solution fails your tests, the test is wrong: fix the test, not the solution.
assertIsNotNone(is_leap_year(2024), msg=...) fails when the function returns None, as it does when it prints instead of returning, so its message can say exactly that.
The checker runs python -m unittest for you, so a test it can't import, or a typo in the test file, shows as no tests run.

modules.title: Try it, share it and make it better
modules.summary: Try your course as a learner, pilot it with a real learner, share it as an archive or on JetBrains Marketplace, and design exercises and feedback that teach.

lessons.title: Try your course as a learner
objectives: Preview a course the way learners will see it
Check each task with wrong and with unexpected right answers
Pilot a course with real learners
key_points: A course preview opens your course in learner mode, in a separate project, so you see what learners will: descriptions, placeholders, hints and the messages from failed checks.
Check every task twice: once with a wrong or empty answer, to read the feedback, and once with a right answer that's different from yours, to make sure the tests don't demand your way of doing it.
In the preview, make sure learners can see every file they need, and can't see what they shouldn't, such as your solution.
A pilot with even a few real learners shows where they get stuck; watch them work, ask them to think aloud, and note where they hesitate.
Fix the biggest problems first: an unclear description or a missing step usually costs learners more time than a typo.

steps.do: Right-click the course in the Project tool window and look for Create Course Preview, in a submenu named after the plugin or Course Creator depending on the version, or find it with Find Action.
steps.see: A new window with the course in learner mode.

steps.do: Open leap_years.
steps.see: The placeholder shows pass, and the hints are folded.

steps.do: Click Check without changing anything.
steps.see: The task isn't solved, and the message is one of yours.

steps.do: Solve it differently from your solution, with one Boolean expression, and click Check again.
steps.see: Solved: the tests check the result, not the method.

steps.do: Close the preview's window. Nothing you did there changes your course.

lessons.title: Share your course
objectives: Export a course as an archive learners can open
Describe how courses are published on JetBrains Marketplace
Keep a course's source in version control
key_points: A course archive is a single file the plugin makes from your course; learners open it from the plugin's course catalogue with its option to open a course from disk.
Courses can also be published on JetBrains Marketplace, where learners find them in the plugin's catalogue; publishing needs a JetBrains account, and you can upload new versions later.
Keep the course project in Git like any code, so you can review changes, work with co-authors and go back to earlier versions.
Say how others may use your course by choosing a licence for its text and code, and include only material you have the right to share.
Before each release, preview the course again and check every task, since a change to one task can affect the tasks after it, especially in a framework lesson.

walkthrough.title: Create a course archive and open it

steps.do: Find Create Course Archive: right-click the course and look in the submenu named after the plugin or Course Creator, or use Find Action.
Choose where to save the archive and name it, such as python-warm-ups.zip.
Open the course catalogue, choose the option to open a course from disk, and select the archive.
steps.see: The course opens as a learner would get it.

steps.do: Back in your course project, commit your work to Git.

lessons.title: Designing exercises and feedback that teach
objectives: Sequence tasks from worked examples to independent practice
Size tasks so each practises one new idea
Write feedback that's specific, actionable and kind
key_points: Start from outcomes: decide what learners should be able to do at the end, then design tasks that practise exactly that, and checks that show they can.
Move from support to independence: a worked example to read and run, then a task that completes a partly written solution, then one written from scratch.
Give each task one new idea and a size learners can finish in a few minutes; a task that needs two new ideas usually works better as two tasks.
Feedback teaches when it's specific (what went wrong, for which input), actionable (what to look at next) and kind; a bare 'wrong answer' teaches nothing.
Return to earlier ideas in later tasks, so learners keep using what they've learnt instead of meeting each idea once.
Let learners' work guide changes: the tasks that many learners fail, or check again and again, are the ones to clarify or split.

lab.title: Pilot your course and ship it
lab.goal: Preview your course, pilot it with one learner, improve it from what you see, and export it as a course archive.
setup: Your Python Warm-ups course, with the leap_years task from module 3
Someone who could take the course, such as a friend or colleague learning Python; if no one is free, take it yourself as if you were new to Python

steps.do: Create a course preview, with Find Action if you need it.
In the preview, try each task with a wrong answer and with a right answer that differs from yours. Note what happens in pilot_report.md.
Ask your learner to take the course while thinking aloud. Don't help unless they're stuck for several minutes; note where they hesitate, what they read, and how long each task takes.
Make at least two improvements based on what you saw, such as a clearer sentence, a new hint, a better message in a test, or a task split in two.
Run the leap-years checker again, to make sure your changes kept its tests working.
steps.see: 3 of 3 wrong answers caught.

steps.do: Create the course archive, with Find Action if you need it, and open it from disk to check it.
Commit the improved course to Git.

checks.text: Every task was tried in the preview with a wrong answer and with a different right answer.
The pilot report says where the learner got stuck, and why.
At least two improvements were made, each following from something seen in the pilot.
The leap-years tests still catch every wrong answer.

lab.submit: Paste your completed pilot_report.md, including the archive's file name, and the checker's output.

# Pilot report

## Who tried the course
<!-- Their background, and whether they thought aloud as they worked. -->

## Preview checks
<!-- For each task: what happened with a wrong answer, and with a right answer that's different from yours. -->

## Where they got stuck
<!-- The task, what happened, how long it took, and which messages or hints they read. -->

## Improvements
<!-- At least two changes, each with the observation that led to it. -->

## Archive
<!-- The file name of the course archive you created. -->

hints: Watching without helping is hard; note the moment you wanted to help, as it usually marks a gap in the course.
If the archive won't open, preview the course again: the preview shows problems sooner.

project.title: Create a mini-course for your learners
project.brief: Design, build, pilot and share a short course in the JetBrains Academy plugin for learners you know or can picture clearly, such as a class, a team or a club. Choose a language the plugin supports and a topic learners can complete in about an hour. The course needs at least two lessons and six tasks, including at least one theory task, three programming tasks checked by tests, and one quiz. Every programming task needs a description with examples and edge cases, starter code with answer placeholders, and tests whose messages tell learners what to fix. For each programming task, write at least two typical wrong answers and show that your tests catch them, as the leap-years checker did. Try the course in a preview, pilot it with at least one learner, improve it, and export it as a course archive.
deliverables: A course plan: the audience, three outcomes, and the tasks in order with the idea each practises
The course project, in a Git repository or as a course archive
For each programming task: its description, its tests, and the results of running them against your solution and the typical wrong answers
A pilot report: what the learner did, where they got stuck and what you changed
A design rationale of up to 400 words: how the tasks build from support to independence, and how the feedback helps

rubric.name: Course structure and design
rubric.description: Clear outcomes; tasks in a sensible order from worked examples to independent practice, one new idea at a time; at least a theory task, three programming tasks and a quiz.

rubric.name: Descriptions and starter code
rubric.description: Descriptions say what to do, with examples and edge cases; starter code runs; placeholders mark exactly what learners write; hints go from a nudge to a bigger step.

rubric.name: Tests and feedback
rubric.description: Tests pass the reference solution and a different correct one, catch every listed wrong answer, check behaviour rather than method, and give messages that say what to fix.

rubric.name: Piloting and improvement
rubric.description: The pilot report is specific, and the changes made follow from what it found.

rubric.name: Sharing
rubric.description: The course is exported as an archive or published, and opens and works for a learner.

project.submit: Paste your course plan, each programming task's description and tests, the results of running the tests against your solution and the wrong answers, your pilot report and design rationale, and a link to the repository or the archive's file name.
